content: Efantine Tablets should be administered with caution in patients who are taking antiretroviral drugs, such as HIV protease inhibitors and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors. This is because these medications may lead to reduced concentrations of artemether, dihydroartemisinin (DHA), and/or lumefantrine, potentially decreasing the antimalarial efficacy of the combination therapy. Additionally, increased lumefantrine concentrations may result in QT interval prolongation. No clinical studies have been conducted to evaluate drug-drug interactions between artemether-lumefantrine tablets and hormonal contraceptives. However, in vitro studies have shown that the metabolism of ethinyl estradiol and levonorgestrel is not induced by artemether, DHA, or lumefantrine. Despite this, artemether has been reported to weakly induce the activity of CYP2C19, CYP2B6, and CYP3A enzymes in humans. Consequently, coadministration of artemether-lumefantrine tablets may potentially reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives. In a parallel-group study involving healthy adult volunteers (n=42 per group), which included placebo and moxifloxacin control groups, administration of a six-dose regimen of artemether-lumefantrine tablets was associated with a QTcF (Fridericia) prolongation of 5 milliseconds (one-sided 95% upper confidence interval: 11 milliseconds). A concentration-dependent increase in QTcF was observed for lumefantrine. In clinical trials conducted in children, no patient exhibited a QTcF interval exceeding 500 milliseconds. However, over 5% of patients experienced a QTcF increase of more than 60 milliseconds. Among adults, over 6% had a QTcF increase of more than 60 milliseconds from baseline. Carcinogenicity studies have not been conducted for the artemether-lumefantrine combination. No evidence of mutagenicity was detected in various tests, including the Salmonella and Escherichia/mammalian-microsome mutagenicity test, the gene mutation test with Chinese hamster V79 cells, the cytogenetic test on Chinese hamster cells in vitro, and the rat micronucleus test in vivo. In reproductive toxicity studies, female rats dosed with the artemether-lumefantrine combination at 1000 mg/kg (approximately nine times the clinical dose based on body surface area) for 2 to 4 weeks exhibited a reduction in pregnancy rates by approximately 50%. Male rats dosed for 70 days showed an increase in abnormal sperm (87% abnormal) and increased testicular weights at doses of 30 mg/kg (approximately one-third of the clinical dose). Higher doses (approximately nine times the clinical dose) resulted in decreased sperm motility and 100% abnormal sperm cells. Neonatal rats (7 to 21 days old) were found to be more sensitive to the toxic effects of artemether, a component of the artemether-lumefantrine combination, compared to older juvenile rats or adults. Mortality and severe clinical signs were observed in neonatal rats at doses that were well tolerated in pups older than 22 days. The efficacy of artemether-lumefantrine tablets was evaluated for the treatment of acute, uncomplicated malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum in HIV-negative patients across eight clinical studies. Uncomplicated malaria was defined as symptomatic P. falciparum malaria without signs or symptoms of severe malaria or evidence of vital organ dysfunction. The majority of patients had parasitemia levels ranging from 0.1% to 4%. These studies were conducted in partially immune and non-immune adults and children (weighing ≥5 kg) with uncomplicated malaria in regions such as China, Thailand, sub-Saharan Africa, Europe, and South America. Patients with clinical features of severe malaria or severe cardiac, renal, or hepatic impairment were excluded from these studies.
